Before Tap Behavior

Before Tap Behaviors allow engineers to observe immutable pipeline state and perform side effects immediately before reducer execution. Before taps are strictly observational: they may log, emit metrics, trigger external effects, or collect diagnostics, but they may not mutate state, alter pipeline execution, or influence snapshot emission.

Before Tap Contract Summary

  • Before tap functions may perform side effects
  • Before tap functions must not mutate the incoming value
  • Before tap functions do not return a value
  • Before tap functions execute in initialization order
  • Errors thrown during tap execution propagate as Vault errors

The Before Tap contract guarantees that tap execution is observational and isolated. If a before tap function throws an error, that error is promoted to a Vault error and immediately terminates the current pipeline execution. The in-flight candidate value is discarded, no reducers are executed, and no snapshot is emitted. This ensures that side-effect failures never result in partially applied state or inconsistent pipeline outcomes.

Before taps participate exclusively in observation and side-effect execution. They do not derive values, do not mutate pipeline state, do not influence control flow, and do not emit snapshots. Their sole responsibility is to observe pipeline values at a precise execution point and react externally.

Before Tap Stage

The Before Tap stage executes immediately after filtering and before reducer execution. Before tap functions receive an immutable snapshot of the current pipeline value and are invoked strictly for observation and side-effect execution.

Tap callbacks are invoked with the current upstream pipeline value. This value is read-only and must not be modified. Any attempt to mutate the value violates pipeline safety guarantees.

Before Taps may:

  • Observe the pipeline value
  • Log or trace execution
  • Emit metrics or diagnostics
  • Trigger external side effects

Before taps do not return values, do not influence control flow, and do not affect snapshot emission. Pipeline execution always continues unchanged following before tap execution unless an error is thrown.

Core Pipeline Stage

The Before Tap stage is a core pipeline stage and is always present in the FeatureCell lifecycle. Individual before tap functions are not declared as part of static FeatureCell configuration. Instead, they are registered explicitly during initialization using the fluent .beforeTaps() API.

Fluent beforeTaps() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple before taps. The .beforeTaps() API accepts an ordered array of tap functions, which are executed sequentially in the Processing Layer in the order they are provided. An empty beforeTaps array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied Before Tap Functions

Before tap functions are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively within the Before Tap stage. They are intended to observe pipeline state at a precise execution boundary and react externally.

Note

Because before taps allow side effects, their logic should remain narrowly focused and intentional. Long-running, blocking, or stateful operations can degrade pipeline performance and introduce hidden coupling. Before taps are most effective when each function performs a single, well-defined observational task such as logging, diagnostics, auditing, or external signaling—not business logic or state derivation.

Before Tap Stage Diagram
Before Tap Behavior

The Before Tap stage is a core pipeline stage and is always present. Engineers supply tap callback functions that are executed by the core before tap behavior during pipeline evaluation.

FeatureCell Initialization

The BeforeTap stage exposes a fluent configuration API that allows engineers to register tap functions during FeatureCell initialization.

This API does not execute tap functions directly. It records an ordered set of before-tap callbacks that are later invoked by the BeforeTap stage after state reduction and snapshot emission.

Registering the beforeTap Behavior

The Tap Behavior is attached structurally when the FeatureCell is initialized using the Fluent Api .beforeTaps method. This determines that the FeatureCell participates in an before-tap-based post-filter execution control at runtime.

Example: Registering Before Tap Callbacks

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService
      {  
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: []
      }
    )
  ]
};

@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more before taps during initialization
    this.vault
      .beforeTaps(
        [
          fn
        ]
      ).initialize()
  }
}`}}
 
{{`export const employeeCell = FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: [],
  }
);

employeeCell
  .beforeTaps(
    [
      fn
    ]
  )
  .initialize();`}}
Before Tap Function Patterns

While JavaScript allows many ways to express a function, only a limited set of patterns are appropriate for tap execution. Because taps allow side effects, function structure and binding discipline are especially important.

The following categories describe the supported and discouraged ways to supply tap functions, ordered from most to least preferred.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure tap functions depend only on their input value and perform deterministic side effect behavior. They do not reference this, do not close over mutable external state, and are fully predictable across executions.

This is the safest and most reusable form of tap function and is recommended whenever possible.

Example 1: Pure Tap Function

{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      console.info('BeforeTap:', current);
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// observes current pipeline value without mutation`}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Tap Function

{{`export function createLoggingTap(label: string) {
  return (current) => {
    console.info(label, current);
  };
}

employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    createLoggingTap('Employee snapshot')
  ]
).initialize();`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Tap Functions (Acceptable)

Tap functions may reference instance state as long as they are correctly bound to the owning instance. These taps are deterministic per FeatureCell instance, but they must not be shared across FeatureCells.

This pattern is acceptable when tap behavior depends on configuration values or services owned by the containing class.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly logPrefix = '[BeforeTap]';

readonly loggingTap = (current) => {
  console.info(this.logPrefix, current);
};

employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [this.loggingTap]
).initialize();`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public logCurrentState(current) {
  console.info('BeforeTap:', current);
}

employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [this.logCurrentState.bind(this)]
).initialize();

// tap is instance-bound and deterministic per FeatureCell`}}

Category C: Delegating Tap Functions

Tap functions may delegate their implementation to helper methods or utilities, provided that those methods remain side-effect-safe and operate only on the provided value.

Because taps do not influence pipeline control flow or state mutation, delegation is safe as long as the delegated logic does not depend on external mutable state or attempt to modify the pipeline value.

This pattern is useful for organizing complex observability logic or sharing instrumentation across taps.

Example 5: Delegating Tap Method

{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => this.logSnapshot(current)
  ]
).initialize();

// tap logic is delegated but remains safe and deterministic`}}

Category D: Inline Lambda Taps (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline lambda functions are allowed, but they are easier to misuse. Because they are often written inline, it is easy to accidentally close over mutable variables or embed complex logic that is difficult to test or reuse.

Inline taps are best reserved for trivial, self-contained observations.

Example 6: Inline Conditional Tap

{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      if (!current?.items?.length) return;
      console.info('Items present:', current.items);
    }
  ]
).initialize();`}}
Before Tap Anti-Patterns

Before taps are observational hooks. They are explicitly designed for side effects, but misuse can degrade pipeline safety, performance, and correctness. The following patterns violate the intent of the Before Tap stage and should be avoided.

Common Anti-Patterns

  • Mutating the pipeline value
  • Performing long-running or blocking operations
  • Encoding business logic or decision-making
  • Depending on external mutable state
  • Assuming tap execution affects pipeline flow

Unlike reducers, tap violations are not always mechanically detectable. Most errors manifest as degraded performance, unexpected coupling, or incorrect assumptions about pipeline behavior.

Example: Discouraged Mutation Inside a Tap

{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      // ❌ Mutating the pipeline value
      current.count++;
      console.info('Mutated count:', current.count);
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// ❌ Violates tap contract: pipeline values are immutable snapshots`}}

Even if this mutation appears to “work,” it violates pipeline guarantees and may corrupt downstream assumptions. Before taps must treat the pipeline value as immutable.

Before Tap Function Summary

Before Tap Function Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the before tap function styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in reusability, testability, and long-term safety.

Before Tap Function Characteristics
Dimension Examples 1 / 2
Pure Tap Functions 		Examples 3 / 4
Instance-Bound Taps 		Example 5
Delegating Tap 		Example 6
Inline Lambda Tap 		Anti-Patterns
Mutation / Blocking / External State
Determinism ✅ ⚠️ Per instance ⚠️ Per instance ⚠️ ❌
Pipeline Safety ✅ ✅ ✅ ⚠️ ❌
Side-Effect Discipline ✅ Minimal / predictable ⚠️ Instance-coupled ⚠️ Delegated ⚠️ Easy to bloat ❌ Unbounded / unsafe
Reusability High Medium Medium Low None
Testability High Medium High Lower Low
Risk of Accidental Closure Low Low Low Higher High
Operational Risk Low Medium Medium Higher High
Intended Lifespan Long-lived Instance-limited Instance-limited Ephemeral Unacceptable
Recommended Usage Preferred Acceptable Acceptable Use sparingly Discouraged

Summary Rule

Any before tap function must treat the pipeline value as immutable and should keep side effects bounded and intentional. Taps may be instance-aware or delegated, but they must not mutate the pipeline value, depend on external mutable variables, or perform long-running/blocking work. Tap behavior should remain deterministic within the owning FeatureCell.

Examples

The following examples demonstrate valid and invalid uses of before tap functions. Before taps are observational hooks: they may read and react to the current pipeline value, but they must not return values or mutate state.

Example 1: Logging the State

{{`@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more beforeTaps during initialization
    this.vault
      .beforeTaps(
        [
          (current) => {
            console.info('State after filters:', current);
          }
        ]
      ).initialize();
  }
}

// logs the current pipeline value without mutation`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      console.info('State after filters:', current);
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// logs the current pipeline value without mutation`}}

Example 2: Measuring State Size

{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(

// emits diagnostic metrics based on snapshot size`}}

Example 3: Snapshot Inspection

{{`@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more beforeTaps during initialization
    this.vault
      .beforeTaps(
        [
          (current) => {
            if (current.items?.length > 100) {
              console.warn('Large state detected');
            }
          }
        ]
      ).initialize();
  }
}

// inspects snapshot and emits a warning when thresholds are exceeded`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      if (current.items?.length > 100) {
        console.warn('Large state detected');
      }
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// inspects snapshot and emits a warning when thresholds are exceeded`}}

Example 4: Invalid — Attempting to Modify State

{{`@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more beforeTaps during initialization
    this.vault
      .beforeTaps(
        [
          (current) => {
            current.count++; // ❌ mutation attempt
          }
        ]
      ).initialize();
  }
}

// ❌ Vault error: tap functions must not mutate state`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      current.count++; // ❌ mutation attempt
    }
  ]
).initialize();

// ❌ Vault error: tap functions must not mutate state`}}

Example 5: Invalid — Returning a New Value

{{`@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[][]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[][]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more beforeTaps during initialization
    this.vault
      .beforeTaps(
        [
          (current) => {
            return { ...current, injected: true }; // ❌ returning a value
          }
        ]
      ).initialize();
  }
}

// ❌ Vault error: tap functions must not return or replace state`}}
 
{{`employeeCell.beforeTaps(
  [
    (current) => {
      return { ...current, injected: true }; // ❌ returning a value
    }
  ]

// ❌ Vault error: tap functions must not return or replace state`}}
